Mediation, Arbitration & Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) in Nepal

Court litigation can be time-consuming, adversarial, and public. We offer skilled, confidential Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) representation in commercial arbitration and professional mediation under the Mediation Act 2068 and Arbitration Act 2055. We help corporate entities, partners, and families resolve high-stakes disputes amicably, efficiently, and with binding legal enforceability.

Request a Consultation Call Chambers: 9745875449 / 9852057087

Understanding the Legal Problem & Client Need

Traditional court proceedings in Nepal often stretch over several years through multiple layers of appeal, straining commercial relationships and eroding capital. Alternative Dispute Resolution offers a sophisticated, private, and expedited alternative. Under the Mediation Act 2068, mediated settlement deeds (Milapatra) carry the full binding force of a final court decree with zero risk of subsequent appeal. In commercial agreements, incorporating modern arbitration clauses under the Arbitration Act 2055 ensures disputes are resolved before neutral industry experts rather than congested court dockets.

Situations Where this Service is Relevant

  • ⚖Commercial partnership and shareholder disputes requiring confidential resolution without public exposure
  • ⚖Contractual construction, supplier, and joint venture disputes with arbitration covenants
  • ⚖Family matrimonial property, inheritance, and business succession disputes requiring delicate handling
  • ⚖Court-annexed mediation mandated during ongoing District Court civil lawsuits
  • ⚖Drafting customized dispute escalation, mediation, and institutional arbitration clauses in commercial contracts
  • ⚖Enforcing domestic arbitral awards or executing mediated settlement agreements in court

Scope of Legal Assistance Offered by our Chambers

  • ✔Representing corporate or individual parties in domestic commercial arbitration proceedings under NEPCA rules
  • ✔Acting as trained party advocates or neutral court-appointed mediators under the Mediation Act 2068
  • ✔Drafting binding, unambiguous Mediated Settlement Agreements (Milapatra Likhit)
  • ✔Submitting mediated settlement deeds to competent courts for immediate formal decree registration
  • ✔Challenging or enforcing arbitral awards before the High Court under the Arbitration Act 2055
  • ✔Conducting pre-dispute settlement negotiations and structured conciliation meetings

Typical Legal Process & Procedural Stages in Nepal

Our advocates guide clients step-by-step through each statutory stage mandated by Nepalese court rules:

1

Dispute Analysis & ADR Appropriateness

Assessing whether the dispute is legally eligible for mediation or arbitration, reviewing contract arbitration clauses, and identifying common interests.
Estimated Timeline: 2 – 4 Days

2

Mediator / Arbitrator Selection

Agreeing upon certified mediators or constituting the arbitral tribunal under the Arbitration Act 2055 or NEPCA rules.
Estimated Timeline: 1 – 2 Weeks

3

Mediation Sessions / Arbitral Hearings

Conducting structured, confidential dialogue, interest-based bargaining, and presenting legal arguments and factual submissions.
Estimated Timeline: 2 Weeks – 3 Months

4

Settlement Deed Drafting / Arbitral Award

Formulating comprehensive, legally binding settlement terms (Milapatra) or receiving the formal Arbitral Award.
Estimated Timeline: 1 – 2 Weeks

5

Court Formalization & Decree Execution

Recording the settlement with the court or enforcing the arbitral award as a final judicial decree.
Estimated Timeline: 1 – 2 Weeks post-execution

Documents & Information Clients May Need to Provide

  • ✔ Underlying contracts, leases, or deeds containing the arbitration or dispute resolution clause
  • ✔ Chronological summary of disputed claims, financial figures, and communications
  • ✔ Identification documents and board resolutions authorizing representation in mediation/arbitration
  • ✔ Copies of court pleadings (if mediation is court-annexed)

Applicable Nepal Legislation & Statutory Authority

Statute / Act Key Provisions / Sections Legal Relevance
Mediation Act 2068 (मध्यस्थता ऐन, २०६८)
Arbitration Act 2055 (मध्यस्थ ऐन, २०५५)
Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074

Important Legal Rights, Duties & Procedural Limitations

  • • Strict Confidentiality: Under Section 22 of the Mediation Act 2068, all statements, admissions, and settlement proposals made during mediation are strictly confidential and inadmissible in subsequent court litigation.
  • • Finality of Settlement: Once a mediated settlement deed (Milapatra) is recorded before a court, it carries the status of a final decree and cannot be appealed.
  • • Arbitrability Limits: Matters involving criminal prosecution, fundamental constitutional rights, or non-compoundable public interest issues cannot be resolved through arbitration.

Factors Affecting Legal Fees & Costs

In accordance with ethical practice in Nepal, our chambers do not publish arbitrary flat fees because every dispute is shaped by distinct evidentiary factors:

  • • Format of dispute resolution (informal commercial mediation vs. full institutional arbitration tribunal)
  • • Number of hearing sessions, mediator/arbitrator honorariums, and venue logistics
  • • Complexity and financial quantum of the commercial claims

What Information to Prepare Before Your Consultation

  • ✔ Review your commercial contract to see if it mandates arbitration or mediation prior to court action
  • ✔ Define your walk-away position, core business priorities, and acceptable settlement compromises
  • ✔ Prepare a clean schedule of damages or financial claims

Common Questions Regarding Mediation & Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)

Is a mediated settlement deed legally binding and enforceable in Nepal?

Yes. Under the Mediation Act 2068 and Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074, a settlement deed (Milapatra) agreed upon by parties and endorsed by the court has the exact same legal force as a judgment decree issued after a full trial, and can be directly executed through court bailiffs.

How does commercial arbitration differ from ordinary court litigation in Nepal?

Arbitration is a private, confidential process where parties select expert arbitrators (often senior advocates, retired judges, or engineers) to adjudicate disputes under flexible procedural timetables. Unlike court litigation which can face multi-tiered appeals, an arbitral award is final and subject to very narrow challenge grounds under the Arbitration Act 2055.
